Carbon Law Group · progress report

Aprende y Planea:
progress report

Phases 1–4 of 8 complete18 November 2026Not yet live with clients

Aprende y Planea is the firm's new Spanish-first, bilingual client app, on the web and as a Chrome extension. Over about two weeks, while the firm prepares the client's will, three animated characters (La Calavera, El Oso and Piñata) teach estate planning in short daily lessons. Each finished lesson takes $100 off the will. Four of the eight phases are now complete. A client can sign up, meet the characters and take every lesson, with each legal point linked to its official California source. The app is not live with clients yet: the conversation, payment, attorney review and signing steps come in Phases 5–8.

The one thing we need

The attorney's review of the lesson content. Clients can't see any lesson until he approves it, and the review packet is ready: 111 legal statements, each with its source and an approval box.

What we built

Phases 1 and 2: the plan and the foundations

Each phase ended with a written report and screenshots, and the next phase started only after the firm said go.

1Plan

Approved by the firm on 17 November 2026, before any code was written
  • A product spec, the technical design and the visual design, including screen mockups and the three characters.
  • A plan of 61 tasks for Phases 2–8, each with tests that define “done”.
  • A list of questions only the firm can answer. Five are already answered: “about two weeks” as the promise, the AI provider approval covering this app, no paid voice server for now, no Stripe account yet, and a higher AI budget.
  • A decision log that records every choice and the reason for it.
Phase 1 design mockup of the course map.

2Foundations

12 tasks, plus one fix to the deployment
  • Accounts and sign-in for clients (adults only), with the app shell in Spanish and English.
  • The client's path, enforced by the server: AI disclosure, then consent, then a names-only conflict check, then personal details. A possible conflict stops everything. Payment needs the firm's clearance, the attorney's scope approval and a signed engagement letter. Documents stay hidden until the attorney approves them.
  • A Chrome extension that runs the app in a side panel, plus a small toolbar popup that shows today's step.
  • Automatic checks on every change. The intake logic from the earlier prototype was moved over unchanged, and tests prove it still behaves the same.
The welcome screen, as it runs today.

What we built

Phases 3 and 4: the characters and the lessons

3Characters

7 tasks
  • Three animated 3D characters: La Calavera (the guide), Piñata (runs the games) and El Oso (the calm voice for the health care lesson). Each one celebrates, thinks and talks.
  • Every character always carries the label “Programa de IA · no es el abogado” (an AI program, not the lawyer).
  • La Calavera's file shrank from 11 MB to 1.3 MB with no visible change. Without 3D support, the app shows still images instead.
  • The characters speak with the device's built-in voice, so there's no voice server to pay for.
The final characters and their expressions.

4Learning

8 tasks merged; the Spanish review is with the firm
  • A course map and a lesson player with six kinds of question: multiple choice, real-life scenarios, true/false, match the pairs, put the steps in order, and listen and answer.
  • 130 lesson items in Spanish and English, covering the four core lessons, the final lesson and four bonus lessons.
  • 111 legal statements, each linked to a section of the California Probate Code or a California Courts self-help page. Every answer shows its source.
  • Rewards: petals, a daily streak candle, seals, and $100 off the will for each lesson. Wrong answers come back later in the lesson, with no penalty.
A right answer, with its official source linked.

How we built it

A controlled process, with a check at every step

AI does the building, under rules the firm controls. Nothing reaches the main code without review and automatic checks, and no phase starts without the firm's go-ahead.

✓
Two kinds of AI worker. Claude Opus did the design, the characters, the lesson content and the legal review. AI builders wrote first versions of the code, and Opus reviewed every one.
✓
Tests come first. For the most important behavior, tests are written before the feature. A change that only games a test is rejected.
✓
Legal accuracy. Every legal statement cites its source, and the statute text was read on the state's official legislative website.
✓
The firm controls spending and risk. The AI asks before spending money, publishing, or touching real client data. Tests use made-up people only.

What review caught before it reached the main code

  • An early version let payment go through on a signed letter alone, without the firm's conflict clearance. It was fixed, and six tests were added.
  • A builder proposed a paid background server. It was replaced with a free one that runs inside the existing service.
  • An old test was calling the real AI service with the firm's key on every run. Tests can no longer reach any outside service.
  • Builders sometimes changed working code just to make a test pass. Each case was reverted, and review now includes screenshots of every screen.

The attorney-approval rule

No legal content reaches a client until the attorney approves that exact version. If anyone edits an approved item, the edit becomes a new draft that needs approval again. The app enforces this; nobody has to remember it.

What is true today

  • The app runs and has been tested end to end, from sign-up to a finished lesson.
  • It has not been used by real clients.
  • No lesson content is approved yet, so none would be shown to a client.

Not built yet

  • Talking with the characters and the intake (Phase 5).
  • Payment, drafting, attorney review and signing (Phase 6). Payment will be built against a test stand-in until the firm opens a Stripe account.
  • Staff controls, then Store release and polish (Phases 7–8).

Next 30 days

Phase 5: conversation and intake

  • The day-1 screens: the AI disclosure, consent, and the names-only conflict check.
  • “Your details”: after each lesson, the character asks the intake questions in a short conversation.
  • The day-4 summary, where the client checks their answers and confirms which documents they want.
  • The calendar behind the two weeks, with alerts to staff when a step is late.
  • A test set of sample conversations to check the characters stay within their limits.
Spending

Live AI conversations cost money

Phase 5 is the first time the app talks to the AI service for real, and each call costs money. We will ask before running those calls. Voice stays on the device's built-in speech until the firm approves paying for a voice server.

Coming later: Phase 6 (payment) needs a firm-owned Stripe account, a decision on which bank account receives payments, and the attorney's decision on how advance fees are held.
